transcript:
Header:
Date/Time: 2026-06-12 16:00 PT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Reed (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Clara Nguyen (Redwood SE), Jenna Park (Hightower Head of ML), Marcus Lee (Platform Eng), Ravi Singh (Security), Priya Kaur (Data Scientist)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on migrating from OpenAI hosted to Redwood Dedicated; primary concerns: model parity/eval, vLLM/TGI compatibility, latency vs cost tradeoffs, security (KMS, SOC2), and rollout timing. Agreed next steps: share pricing/TCO, schedule technical deep-dive, customer to send eval prompts.

Topics:
- Current usage and pain points with OpenAI
- Compatibility with vLLM/TGI and inference runtime differences
- Eval parity and benchmark methodology
- Networking, KMS, and compliance questions for Dedicated/Private
- Rollout plan and timeline

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Reed: Hey everyone thanks for joining, um we're excited to chat through your migration thinking. quick round-robin? Jenna, do you want to kick off with where Hightower is today?
[00:12] Jenna Park: Yeah thanks Alex. so we're a little over a year into building a couple of LLM features, mostly on OpenAI API. prod traffic is roughly 120k tokens/day right now but peaks at 3x during business hours. main pain is cost unpredictability and occasional latency spikes; also want more control over data residency and audit logs as we move into enterprise customers.
[00:34] Marcus Lee: to add, our infra team wants the ability to pin model versions and run our own quantized runtime eventually, we've been experimenting with vLLM on prem in dev but it's flaky at scale.
[00:46] Samir Patel: yeah that's a pretty common pattern. quick clarifying Q — when you say "vLLM flaky," are you running the open-source vLLM stack yourself or using a hosted variant?
[00:56] Marcus Lee: we're running open-source v L L M on a few GPU nodes, yes, but we hit OOMs and unstable latency under burst.
[01:04] Samir Patel: makes sense. Redwood Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and an inference runtime that tries to avoid those OOM patterns with optimized KV cache and auto batching—sorry, K V cache, auto-batching and padding heuristics.
[01:16] Jenna Park: important for us: eval parity. our product team says outputs with Redwood should match what we see on Open AI within acceptable delta. how do you handle model weights / tokenization differences and random seeds?
[01:28] Clara Nguyen: great question. short answer: we validate on the same model checkpoints where available; for forks or different distributions we run alignment evals. in practice, determinism differs — we provide seed controls and can run multiple sampling configs to reproduce behavior. for quantized variants there's some delta, so we run an eval suite to quantify quality vs cost tradeoff.
[01:50] Priya Kaur: and do you support TGI and the huggingface stack? a lot of our models live as containers we pulled from HF and some teams use text gen inference.
[01:59] Samir Patel: we support compatible model formats; we have integrations for TGI-style containers and we've done migrations from HF/TGI and v L L M. there are a few gotchas — tokenizer mismatches and custom ops. we usually suggest a quick model validation run to confirm parity.
[02:14] Jenna Park: okay, can you walk through a hypothetical benchmark — latency and cost comparisons vs OpenAI?
[02:20] Alex Reed: sure — high level: hosted OpenAI gives you lowest operational lift but variable cost; Dedicated gives predictable throughput/cost and better latency consistency because of reserved capacity. for example, for a 3B-ish model serving with batching tuned for your traffic, we saw median p50 latencies around 150-220ms on Dedicated vs spikes to 400-600ms on shared endpoints in similar workloads. cost per 1k tokens varies based on quantization and batch; we'll share a TCO sheet after this call.
[02:46] Marcus Lee: those numbers assume optimized kernels and NVidia A100s? what hardware are you recommending?
[02:52] Samir Patel: for now we recommend a mix — A100s for highest throughput, H100s for mixed precision workloads; we can tune for your latency SLOs. Dedicated config is flexible — you can allocate GPU pools per route/service.
[03:05] Ravi Singh: security question — we need KMS integration for customer keys, SOC2 reports, SSO via SAML, and audit logs that show per-request data lineage. how does Redwood handle that in Dedicated and Private?
[03:16] Alex Reed: Dedicated supports customer-managed KMS integrations (we have partnerships with AWS KMS and other HSM vendors). we provide audit logs and can integrate with your SIEM; SOC2 Type II docs are available — I'll attach in the follow-up. SSO/SAML and RBAC are supported via our console.
[03:31] Ravi Singh: do you support bringing your own HSM or a vault cluster?
[03:34] Clara Nguyen: yes PWK — sorry, we support BYO-HSM in Private deployments; Dedicated in a cloud region supports KMS chain. we'll capture the exact vendor names in the follow-up.
[03:44] Jenna Park: on the migration path, our main ask is a low-risk pilot that proves eval parity and throughput under our workload. what's a realistic pilot?
[03:52] Samir Patel: typical pilot is 2-4 weeks: we spin up a Dedicated pool, run your eval set through model variants (float16, int8 quantized) and compare outputs, latency, and cost. we often include a small shadow routing of live traffic to verify production behavior.
[04:09] Marcus Lee: how do you handle traffic routing? can we route only a percentage of requests to Dedicated while keeping fallback to OpenAI hosted?
[04:16] Alex Reed: yes — smart routing is built in. you can route by percentage, latency, model capability, or region. fallback to hosted OpenAI or another variant is supported if Dedicated capacity is saturated.
[04:28] Jenna Park: regarding eval parity, what metrics do you produce? BLEU/Rouge isn't enough for us; we have a business metric on hallucination rate and factual accuracy relative to our dataset.
[04:40] Samir Patel: we output distributional metrics (token-level diffs), similarity scores (embedding cosine between outputs), and task-specific metrics you define — hallucination rate measured against labeled ground-truth. we also produce per-prompt latency and cost breakdown which helps decide quantization profiles.
[04:59] Priya Kaur: can we see an example eval report?
[05:02] Alex Reed: yes — we'll share a redwood-eval sample and a benchmark spreadsheet. link: (deck and bench) — we'll attach in email.
[05:10] Jenna Park: about vLLM specifically — our devs like it because it's open and cheap, but production stability concerns are big. are you basically wrapping v L L M under the hood or is this a different runtime?
[05:24] Samir Patel: our runtime evolved from the same OSS ideas — continuous batching, KV cache management — but it's a dedicated inference engine with optimized kernels, and it handles dynamic batching and memory planning differently. we don't just run vanilla vLLM; we do real-time kernel selection and pad/batch heuristics to avoid the OOMs you mentioned.
[05:44] Marcus Lee: does Redwood Dedicated support custom ops or if we have a specialized attention kernel in our HF container?
[05:50] Clara Nguyen: we can support certain custom ops, but there is an onboarding step: we review the container, validate ops, and either add runtime support or recommend a compatibility shim. custom ops slow path is possible but might reduce perf.
[06:03] Jenna Park: licensing — if we have commercial models from a vendor or proprietary weights, is that okay on Dedicated or Private?
[06:10] Alex Reed: yes — customers can bring commercial or proprietary weights to Dedicated or Private. for hosted we have to confirm licensing terms, but Dedicated and Private are customer-owned in terms of model weights and data.
[06:20] Ravi Singh: data retention and logs — can logs be routed to our S3 with lifecycle policies? we need 7-year retention for compliance.
[06:27] Samir Patel: logs can forward to your S3 or existing logging infra, and you can configure retention. we'll document exact retention policies and help set up lifecycle rules.
[06:36] Marcus Lee: do you support on-prem for air-gapped customers? we have a couple of regulated customers where that may be required down the line.
[06:42] Alex Reed: yes — Redwood Private is the on-prem or VPC-deployed control plane option. it supports air-gapped installs with local model hosting. that's a bigger project but doable; we can provide a separate statement of work.
[06:54] Jenna Park: timeline wise, if we wanted to pilot next month, what are the gating items?
[06:59] Alex Reed: primary gating: sign an MSA/PO for Dedicated capacity, provide model artifacts or model names, share eval prompts and traffic profile. from our side, we need access to a test VPC or allow-list IPs for the pilot.
[07:12] Priya Kaur: sample prompts — should they be production prompts or synthetic? we can prep a small canonical set.
[07:18] Samir Patel: production real traffic that's scrubbed is ideal. if you can't share that, a close synthetic set is fine. the goal is to reflect token lengths and distribution so batching behavior matches.
[07:29] Jenna Park: cost question: our procurement will ask for a 12-month commit vs on-demand. how does Redwood price Dedicated?
[07:36] Alex Reed: Dedicated is usually reserved capacity pricing with monthly or annual commits; we offer discounts for multi-year or larger commitments. the TCO sheet will show per-token cost estimates across configs (float16, int8) and amortized infra and SRE costs.
[07:51] Marcus Lee: there's also a question of auto-scaling — if we get a sudden spike, can Dedicated burst to hosted capacity?
[07:58] Clara Nguyen: yes, there's burst to a shared pool option and policy-driven fallback to hosted. you configure burst budgets and fallback rules.
[08:07] Jenna Park: okay let's talk specifics on model compatibility. we run gpt-3.5 style families and a custom LLaMA-variant. will Redwood accept those weights as-is?
[08:18] Samir Patel: we accept LLaMA forks and many gpt-family checkpoints. for certain forks we need to recompile tokenizers or ensure tokenizer configs match, that is part of the onboarding validation. for custom LLaMA variants we often run a quick conversion step.
[08:33] Ravi Singh: legal — any concerns about export controls for specialized weights?
[08:36] Alex Reed: we have a legal process to vet any export control concerns; typically customers sign certs if required and we work with legal. we'll loop in our legal team if you surface specific flags.
[08:48] Priya Kaur: on eval parity: do you support deterministic seeds to make exact output matching? in many generation tasks we rely on sampling and temperature so exact matches are unrealistic.
[08:57] Samir Patel: deterministic seed helps for greedy and top-k scenarios; sampling introduces non-determinism. we focus on behavior parity: distributional similarity, task-level metrics, and flashpoint tests for hallucination/factuality. we can run many-shot comparisons to estimate expected variance.
[09:12] Alex Reed: quick pause — a couple of practical items: we'll send a pricing/TCO, SOC2 artifact, and a bench template. Samir will schedule the technical deep-dive. Jenna, you'll share eval prompts. anything else to capture as immediate asks?
[09:28] Jenna Park: yes please include network requirements for the pilot and a checklist for what we need to prepare in our VPC.
[09:34] Alex Reed: noted.
[09:36] Marcus Lee: on the technical deep-dive, we'd like to show our infra stack — we use GKE + Anthos and have egress controls, so we need specifics on allowed ports and IP ranges.
[09:47] Samir Patel: we'll include a network appendix and an egress firewall checklist in the follow-up.
[09:53] Priya Kaur: one more question — if we quantize to int8 for cost, have you seen certain classes of prompts degrade more than others?
[09:59] Samir Patel: yes, long-context summarization sometimes shows more degradation in int8; instruction-following tasks usually are tolerant. that's why pilot evaluation across your prompt types is critical.
[10:12] Jenna Park: legal and procurement — our procurement will need an SOW and pricing table. can we get a draft SOW?
[10:19] Alex Reed: we'll attach a standard SOW template and a draft tailored to your pilot.
[10:23] Ravi Singh: please also share your incident response playbook high level — we need to know SLAs and escalation paths.
[10:29] Clara Nguyen: we'll include an incident response summary and SLA targets. Dedicated comes with a latency uptime SLA in enterprise plans.
[10:36] Alex Reed: ok we're about 30 minutes in, maybe open the floor for any final deeper technical Qs before we wrap?
[10:42] Marcus Lee: quick perf Q — do you support KV cache warm-up across restarts to avoid cold-start penalties?
[10:47] Samir Patel: yes, we persist and preload KV caches for hot routes and we have prewarming options for models to reduce cold-starts.
[10:56] Priya Kaur: can we control sampling params per-route so product teams can choose deterministic vs creative outputs?
[11:01] Clara Nguyen: yes per-route sampling config is supported in the routing layer, you can pin temperature, top-p, seeds.
[11:09] Jenna Park: in terms of instrumentation, does Redwood provide token-level cost breakdowns visible per request in the console?
[11:15] Alex Reed: yes cost and latency breakdowns per request and per route, and you can export to CSV.
[11:20] Marcus Lee: last operational Q: what does rollback look like if we see a regression after switching traffic to Dedicated?
[11:26] Samir Patel: you can do immediate rollback via routing policies to point back to hosted OpenAI or previous model versions; we also support canary percentages and automatic fallback if error thresholds are exceeded.
[11:38] Jenna Park: perfect. thanks everyone. to recap — Redwood will share pricing/TCO, SOC2 and KMS docs, bench template, and schedule a 1hr deep-dive. Hightower will share eval prompts and traffic profile.
[11:52] Alex Reed: that's it — we'll follow up with links. thanks all.
[12:00] [call ends]
